by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and the asset fits an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as caps, not eligibility thresholds: include § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle and § 33-1125(10) for a firearm even when value exceeds the limit. Include § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), as the homestead exemption alternative. Confirm the statutory category before applying its cap.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel; § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings, and subsection (B) is a one-homestead limitation rather than a separate asset exemption. Non-ring jewelry does not qualify under either § 33-1125(1) or § 33-1125(4).

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate every applicable specific paragraph, then independently include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), which can protect any property. A dollar ceiling limits protection rather than eligibility. Thus a vehicle remains eligible under § 522(d)(2) above its cap, jewelry uses § 522(d)(4), and § 522(d)(5) remains an additional alternative even when a specific paragraph applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) for an unlisted category such as a firearm or jewelry, do not omit a specific paragraph because value exceeds its ceiling, and do not repeat a citation.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is allowable and an eligible asset-exemption pair needs a claim value.
by_task.procedure: Compute each alternative independently. Use the lesser of asset value and $4,450 under § 522(d)(2), $700 per item under § 522(d)(3), or $1,875 under § 522(d)(4). Independently include § 522(d)(5) for every debtor-owned asset: because this is a separate alternative, do not subtract a simultaneously listed § 522(d)(1) claim. Its maximum is $15,425 per debtor ($1,475 plus $13,950), or $30,850 for jointly owned property of two debtors under § 522(m), subject to the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because a specific paragraph applies or because the asset is not a residence. Do not report more than $700 per item under § 522(d)(3), and do not treat that paragraph as covering firearms, jewelry, or other unlisted categories.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the property is held for personal rather than business use.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) independently as the any-other-property alternative, including when apparel, a motor vehicle, or a prescribed health aid also has a specific exemption. Section (a) covers necessary wearing apparel, (c) covers a motor vehicle, and (e) covers professionally prescribed health aids. A value above a limit does not eliminate either applicable alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 12-1001(d) for ordinary household property; it requires implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry or a watch as necessary wearing apparel under subsection (a), and do not omit subsection (b) merely because a specific subsection applies.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and an eligible personal-use asset-exemption pair needs valuation.
by_task.procedure: Compute overlapping alternatives separately. For § 12-1001(b), use the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor, or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. For § 12-1001(c), use the lesser of value and $2,400; this vehicle limit is not doubled. Thus a jointly owned vehicle may have both an $8,000 subsection (b) alternative and a separate $2,400 subsection (c) alternative. Sections (a) and (e) have no stated dollar ceiling in the supplied text, so use the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not assign the $8,000 joint wildcard amount to subsection (c), replace the $2,400 vehicle limit with a wildcard limit, omit subsection (b) because a specific subsection applies, or apply these personal-property exemptions to business-use property.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: After checking every specific Oregon category, make a separate § 18.345(1)(p) check for each item of personal property and include it even when a specific exemption also applies, including for a vehicle, firearm, prescribed health aid, or household good.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute subsection (p) for the specific category, apply it to real property, classify wearing apparel as household goods under § 18.345(1)(f), or use vehicle subsection (d) for nonvehicles.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and § 18.345(1)(p) applies to personal property.
by_task.procedure: Report the § 18.345(1)(p) alternative independently at the lesser of the asset value and $400, including when a vehicle, firearm, health aid, or household good also has a specific Oregon exemption. Retain and value the correct specific alternative separately.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit subsection (p) because the asset exceeds $400 or another subsection applies. Do not classify apparel under subsection (f), use vehicle subsection (d) for household electronics, or replace a specific category with subsection (p).

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and an occupied homestead is jointly owned by two household debtors.
by_task.procedure: Under Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.395(1), report the homestead alternative at the lesser of its value and the $50,000 combined limit. Use the $40,000 limit when only one debtor's homestead interest is involved.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $40,000 single-debtor limit for a jointly owned homestead of two household debtors, and do not apply either homestead limit to personal property.

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the debtor owns the property.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for the property, whether or not a specific federal or Pennsylvania exemption also applies and whether or not the property's value exceeds the monetary limit.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category, use a specific category belonging to a different kind of property, or treat a firearm as wearing apparel under § 8124(a)(1).

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and § 8123 is evaluated.
by_task.procedure: Eligibility under § 8123 does not depend on property category or value. Report one independent alternative at the lesser of asset value and $300 for one debtor, or the lesser of asset value and $600 for jointly owned property of two married debtors.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 for real property, business tools, household goods, appliances, or property already covered federally. Do not report only $300 for jointly owned property of two married debtors, and do not use § 8124(a)(3) unless the property is a qualifying sewing machine.

by_task.when: WISCONSIN is allowable and an eligible personal-use consumer good or motor vehicle needs valuation.
by_task.procedure: For § 815.18(3)(d), use the lesser of value and $12,000 for one debtor, or $24,000 for jointly owned property of two spouses under § 815.18(8). Firearms, animals, apparel, jewelry, appliances, and other listed personal-use goods fall in subsection (d). For a one-debtor motor vehicle under § 815.18(3)(g), independently add the unused $12,000 subsection (d) amount to the $4,000 vehicle amount, giving a maximum of $16,000 subject to vehicle value; do not reduce it for other assets because this task evaluates each pair independently.

delta.noop_reason: No grounded nonregressing delta remains. The current parent already explicitly covers the recurring missing alternatives and amount rules for federal § 522(d)(5), Oregon § 18.345(1)(p), Pennsylvania § 8123, and Illinois § 12-1001(b). Rephrasing those rules previously caused replay regressions, while the attempted Arizona assistive-device and Wisconsin vehicle/consumer-goods additions also failed the required current-and-prior TRAIN gates. Repeating those unsupported edits or adding redundant generic guidance would violate the admission policy.
